Multithreaded match() and %in%

Source: R/par-match.R
par_match.Rd

Same results as base::match() and %in%, but much faster for large inputs. Use as drop-in replacements:

  • par_match() for match().

  • %par_in% for %in%.

Also, par_in() is %par_in% as a regular function. It combines better with the pipe and takes an nthreads argument, so you can fine-tune its performance.

Usage

par_match(
  x,
  table,
  nomatch = NA_integer_,
  incomparables = NULL,
  nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L)
)

x %par_in% table

par_in(x, table, nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L))

Arguments

x

Values to look up.

table

Values to look them up in.

nomatch

The value returned where there is no match, coerced to integer.

incomparables

Values that cannot be matched, as in base::match(). NULL or FALSE means none. Note that using this argument makes the function fall back to base R, so it gets no speedup.

nthreads

A whole number: the max number of threads to use. 0 means the RAYON_NUM_THREADS environment variable, or else all cores. The default is the parvenu.threads option, or 0 if that isn't set. Inputs too small to keep that many threads busy get fewer, and more threads than cores count as all cores.

Value

Just like base match() and %in%:

  • par_match() returns an integer vector containing the first positions of the elements of x in table, or nomatch if an element is not in table.

  • %par_in% and par_in() return a logical vector: TRUE if an element of x is in table, and FALSE if not. They never return NA: an NA in x is TRUE if table contains NA, and FALSE if not.

Details

Speedups result from a Rust implementation using rayon. To use %par_in% within your package, run this once:

usethis::use_import_from("parvenu", "%par_in%")

These functions are computed in parallel when x or table has at least 1e4 elements and both sides are integer, double (in any mix), character, Date, or POSIXct. Factors are matched by their levels. Anything else goes to base::match() unchanged. Strings are matched by their pointers, which the threads read straight from R's memory, as data.table does.

incomparables has some quirks and is rarely used, so it gets no Rust implementation: if it is anything other than NULL or FALSE, the call goes to base::match().

Examples

par_match(c(3, 1, 9), 1:5, nthreads = 2)
#> [1]  3  1 NA
c("b", "z") %par_in% letters
#> [1] TRUE TRUE
par_in(c("b", "z"), letters, nthreads = 2)
#> [1] TRUE TRUE
